title: Ideas built to pass all nine checks
intro: Designed against the nine checks (proven loop, open theme, hook, shareable moment, feel, click, look and sound, timing, return and money), then graded by a critic who re-rated every check, verified the shakiest figures, fixed what could be fixed and cut what couldn't. Ordered by the critic's judgement of each idea's chance to win. None is a sure thing; each one's 'Prove it first' test tells you cheaply whether strangers agree.

winners.name: Scuff & Shine
winners.theme: Small-object restoration with nostalgia: beloved everyday sneakers
winners.hook: Grandpa's mud-grey 1985 runners: one brush stroke cuts a white stripe, one towel wipe brings the whole side back, and you decide which scuffs are memories.
winners.oneLiner: Run a one-bench shoe restoration shop in the back room of a tiny shopfront: open each shoebox and its owner's note, scrub and wipe away decades of grime, de-yellow soles on the windowsill, re-glue, re-paint and re-lace, and protect the marks that matter (a kid's name on the tongue, a friend's doodle on the toe) before the pair goes home.

clipStoryboard.shot: Tight on a mud-caked grey runner on a green cutting mat under a warm gooseneck lamp; a soapy brush hovers. Heard: a dull rubber thud and a cardboard box lid.
One brush stroke along the midsole cracks the dry crust and leaves a single shocking pale stripe through the grime. Heard: a wet bristle 'shff' and a crust crackle.

Small circles build a thick lather that turns brown as it lifts the dirt; then a towel sweeps once and the whole side flashes white, a glint running along the wipe edge. The towel comes away brown. Heard: foam fizz, rubber squeak, a soft tuned 'ting'.
Hold on the split shoe: half mud, half gleaming, with a strip of blue painter's tape protecting a child's marker name on the tongue.
The yellowed sole, wrapped in cling film on a sunny windowsill, timelapses from nicotine yellow to icy translucent blue.
The finished pair goes back into its box beside an old photo of the owner wearing them; the lid closes. Heard: the zone 'tings' resolve into one warm chord.

provenLoop.loop: Take in a dirty, worn object with a story, clean and restore it in tool passes until every zone is done, return it, earn better tools and harder jobs (the PowerWash / ReStory / House Flipper restoration loop).

openTheme.demand: Sneaker cleaning and restoration is one of the biggest evergreen before-and-after formats on YouTube and TikTok: Reshoevn8r's Vick Almighty has about 1.6M YouTube subscribers and 803K Instagram followers (Viral Nation; confirmed by search; a separate 2.4M TikTok figure could not be confirmed and is dropped). The research names nostalgic small-object restoration as the fastest-growing open pocket (ReStory 500k+). Caution: that audience skews toward sneaker culture rather than cozy gamers, so the owner stories have to bridge the two.
openTheme.supply: No dedicated sneaker restoration game found in two rounds of searching. Shoemaker (Steam, 2018, $0.99) is a tiny boot-repair game with no visible audience; mobile has hypercasual 'shoe DIY' ad games; Sneaker Store Simulator and Shoes Store Simulator are reportedly retail stocking sims (designer search, not re-confirmed). The real threat is generalist restorers: The Repair House (by the PC Building Simulator creator; instruments, arcade cabinets, antiques, toys), Cozy Game Restoration (cartridges, Sept 2026), Workshop Simulator (Mixed, 307 reviews) and Things Left Unsaid (2027). Any of them could add a shoe level, so the sneaker game must be the best at one object, not broader.
openTheme.searched: Searched 'sneaker restoration simulator Steam game cleaning shoes', 'sneaker cleaning restoration simulator game Steam' (only The Repair House, a generalist, came up), '"sneaker restoration" game Steam OR itch.io', 'Vick Almighty Reshoevn8r subscribers' and '"Scuff & Shine" game Steam'. No sneaker restorer exists; the name is free.

coreAction.verb: Scrub, then wipe (the brush cracks the crust and lifts grime into foam; one towel pass reveals the clean)
coreAction.input: Mouse: hold left button and scrub; small circles clean fastest (real technique), long strokes leave streaks. Right button + drag is the towel wipe. Wheel or Q/E turns the shoe held in your off-hand between 6 framed angles. Controller: right stick scrubs at the reticle, right-trigger pressure sets brush pressure, left trigger + flick wipes, left stick turns the shoe. Touch (browser slice): one finger scrubs, a two-finger swipe wipes.
coreAction.response: Within one frame the brush head lands where you point and its bristles splay against the direction of travel. On caked mud the first pass cracks the crust and leaves a pale stripe (guaranteed, for the clip). Foam spawns exactly at the contact point and starts tinting toward the colour of the dirt it lifts. Within about 80 ms the material squeak starts, pitched by stroke speed, and the shoe nudges a few millimetres in your hand from the force. The grime mask thins one layer per pass (crust, then grime, then stain), so progress shows under your hand but the full clean waits for the towel.
feedback: First-stroke crack: on a fresh shoe the first pass on dry mud breaks the crust into a pale stripe with a crackle and a few dry flakes. It promises the clean without giving it away, and it is the clip's opening beat.

Bristle splay and follow-through: bristles bend opposite to motion with a 60–80 ms spring lag, flick back with overshoot when you change direction or lift, and throw 2–4 droplets; the head tilts to hug the midsole curve.

Dirty foam as the progress readout: lather grows with scrub speed, takes on the colour of what it lifts (white, grey, brown) and slowly slides down under gravity, so you watch the dirt move from the shoe into the foam.

The wipe, the payoff beat: one towel drag carries the foam away in a smooth wave and exposes everything you cleaned at once, with a specular glint travelling along the wipe edge, a whoosh and a short bright 'shing'. The towel visibly darkens.

Material-aware sound: separate close-mic scrub loops for mesh (crackly fizz), suede (soft hush), leather (squeak) and rubber (high squeal), with pitch and volume tied to stroke speed and ±8% random pitch per stroke; a foam-crackle layer grows with foam volume.

Zone completion: when a zone (toe box, heel tab, midsole wall) passes ~97% it auto-completes with a single light sweep and a soft bell 'ting' tuned to that zone, so a finished shoe plays a little chord. No percentage ever appears.
Rinse bowl: dipping the brush clouds the bowl; over a job it goes from clear to cocoa, an ambient record of how filthy the pair was.

Camera: a 3–5% micro-zoom toward the active area that relaxes when you stop; a 3% ease-in and 0.5 s hold on each wipe; on the last zone the camera eases back to a three-quarter hero view under the lamp. No shake ever.

Love marks: some marks are not dirt (a marker name, a doodle, a signature). They are a fragile layer that fades in visible stages with a soft warning tone if you scrub them; blue painter's tape masks them with a satisfying tear-and-press sound, and a tiny heart pin shows it is protected.

Haptics and UI: controller rumble textured per material (soft on suede, buzzy on mesh, ticks on rubber) with one crisp pulse per zone 'ting'; on screen only a shoebox-lid checklist with pencil ticks (clean, de-yellow, glue, paint, lace) and the owner's note pinned to the lamp.
coreAction.payoff: The towel wipe that turns a brown, foamy panel bright white in one sweep, repeated zone by zone until the shoe glints under the lamp; then secondary verbs in the same feel language (a paint pen that lays a wet line drying matte in 0.5 s, the windowsill de-yellowing timelapse, laces ticking through eyelets) and the box shot beside the owner's old photo.
tuning: firstStrokeContrast: how visible the crust-crack stripe is (must read on a phone screen)
Grime layers per zone (2–4) and removal per pass per material: target 6–12 strokes per zone
circularBonus: how much faster small circles clean than straight strokes, teaching technique without text
Brush radius and edge softness: precise versus forgiving
Foam spawn rate, maximum volume, tint speed and slide speed: how readable 'dirt moving into foam' is
Wipe width and glint travel speed: wide enough to feel like one magic sweep
Bristle spring stiffness and damping (overshoot on lift)
shoeNudge: how far the shoe moves under force (too much feels slippery, zero feels dead)
Love-mark fragility (passes before it fades) and tape stickiness
Zone auto-complete threshold (95–98%) and micro-zoom amount (3–5%)
feelsBadIf: Pixel hunting for the last 1% (PowerWash's known pain point). Fix: zones auto-complete above ~97% with a sweep, and a UV torch shows leftover spots on demand.
The clean appears instantly under the brush, killing the scrub-then-wipe reveal. Fix: the brush only cracks the crust and lifts dirt into foam; the towel reveals.
Scrubbing feels like an eraser tool on a texture. Fix: bristle splay, foam that carries dirt colour, shoe nudge and material sound.
Turning the shoe is fiddly. Fix: snap to 6 framed angles with free rotation between, and 'next dirty zone' auto-turn on request.
A love mark is erased with no warning. Fix: staged fading with a warning tone, and tape always one click away.
Every shoe feels the same. Fix: materials demand different tools (suede eraser and crepe brush dry, mesh with foam, leather with cream), plus damage types and one new tool every few jobs.

Fake brands look cheap, or real ones invite legal trouble. Fix: a small set of lovingly invented, era-true brands with their own logos and history (an '85 runner, an '88 basketball high, a '99 skate shoe, a canvas low).
Grime reads as disgusting. Fix: mud, dust and age only, never bodily.

clickMoment.first: Inside 30 seconds, before any menu: the first stroke cracks a pale stripe through grandpa's mud, a few circles turn the foam brown, and one towel wipe flashes the whole side white. 'It's actually clean under there.' Only then does the note in the box appear: 'These were Dad's. Please keep his name on the tongue,' and the tape is introduced on the spot.
clickMoment.deeper: The deeper click is reading shoes like a restorer (which tool for which material, what to tape, how long the sole sits in the sun) and the first real 'keep' choice: a teenager's court shoes with her late friend's doodle on the toe box, which you clean around and re-edge. Attachment lands with the first owner reply, a photo of the grandad in the restored runners at a wedding, and later with your own swap-meet 'grail' pair on the shelf.

look.short: Back-room cobbler bench · green cutting mat under a warm lamp · soft-stylised shoes with real material texture
look.vibe: A narrow back room behind a tiny shopfront: a green self-healing cutting mat with a white grid, a brass gooseneck lamp, a pegboard of brushes, rolls of blue painter's tape, and a windowsill lined with cling-filmed soles turning in the sun. The shoes are the only saturated things: soft-stylised, slightly chunky proportions with convincing materials (matte suede, glossy leather, honeycomb mesh, a creamy midsole that goes properly white), so grime reads as real and clean reads as factory-fresh. The background falls into warm bokeh; customers exist as notes, voices and old photos.
look.signature: The split shoe: one half mud-brown, the other gleaming white, divided by a crisp line of brown foam, with a strip of blue painter's tape over a child's handwritten name on the tongue.
references: Reshoevn8r / Vick Almighty restoration videos (macro shots, lamp light, foam)
PowerWash Simulator's clean-stripe readability
ReStory's specific nostalgic objects and warm bench
Unpacking (story told through objects)
Product photography of vintage sneakers on cutting mats
avoid: Real brand logos or trademarked silhouettes (swoosh, Jumpman)
Hype-shop streetwear neon and resale 'flex' coldness
Photoreal grime that reads as disgusting or horror-cleaner tones
AI-generated textures, art, voice or music

winners.sound: ASMR-first real foley recorded on thrifted sneakers: per-material bristle scrubs, foam crackle, rubber squeaks, tape tears, lace zips and box lids, all close-mic'd, with the squeak pitch following your hand. Music is warm human-played lo-fi soul with a Rhodes that ducks under every scrub so the brush is the music; the zone 'tings' are a tuned bell set, so finishing a shoe plays a chord.

timing.session: One pair is one job of about 6–10 minutes: unbox and read the note, inspect under the UV torch, dry-brush, scrub and wipe each zone, then glue, paint and re-lace. A shop day is 2–3 pairs plus one sole curing on the windowsill overnight. Weekends add a swap meet where you buy beat-up pairs blind (a 'what's under the mud' reveal) for the shelf or resale. The arc is tool unlocks, harder materials (suede, patent, crumbling vintage foam) and owner storylines that return with follow-ups.
timing.firstMinute: 0–10 s: a box opens on the bench with one muddy runner, a brush and a towel. 10–30 s: first stroke, pale stripe; circles, brown foam; wipe, white side. 30–50 s: the first zone 'tings' and the note appears, introducing the tape. 50–60 s: the shoe turns to show the yellowed sole, the hook into the next tool.
timing.marketWindow: Why now: 2026 is the year of tactile restoration breakouts (ReStory 500k+, Dressmaker #9 global), the object categories are being claimed one by one, and no sneaker restorer exists. Plan: post browser-slice clips during spring 'clean your whites' season, take the Steam demo to the June Steam Next Fest, and launch 1.0 at back-to-school in late summer, when sneaker-cleaning content peaks; send the game to real sneaker restorers for reaction videos as the main launch lever. Spring cleaning season becomes the first anniversary update.

comeBack.short: A yellowed sole is curing on the windowsill, and the next box from a returning owner is on the doorstep with a follow-up note.
comeBack.long: Owner storylines that come back (the nurse's retirement pair, grandpa's wedding shoes), a growing wall of before/after polaroids, tool and technique unlocks (steamers, sole swaps, re-dye, custom paint), swap-meet blind buys with rare finds under the mud, a personal grail shelf, a 'my own pair' sandbox with shareable turntable GIFs, and seasonal jobs (festival boots, salt-stained winter boots, prom and wedding sneakers).

money.model: Free browser toy, then a paid itch.io/Ko-fi supporter build while the Steam page collects wishlists, then premium Steam with a demo; later story-pair and boots/skates DLC and console ports.
money.evidence: PowerWash Simulator 2 sells at $24.99 (~$5.2M est. gross); Dressmaker at $14.99 recouped in under 24h; the genre's implied average realised price is $10–12 (Supermarket Simulator, TCG Card Shop). House Flipper 2 and Gas Station Simulator extend the tail with DLC. Themed sims without a breakout land at 25k–120k copies; a specific nostalgic object (ReStory) broke out at 500k+, while generic cozy repair (Piece by Piece) is estimated at only ~4.8k copies (low confidence). Cozy games reaching 1,000 reviews correspond to roughly $150k gross.

winners.proveItFirst: Build a Three.js browser toy with one commissioned shoe model (one silhouette, three grime layers, three zones, one taped love mark): scrub, lather, wipe, nothing else. Record three caption-free vertical clips (first-stroke stripe, full wipe reveal, before/after with the taped name) and post them twice: once into sneaker-cleaning TikTok/Shorts (tag restorers) and once into cozy-gaming spaces (r/CozyGamers, cozy TikTok). A yes is a clip over 100k views with 'where can I play' comments from BOTH audiences, players posting their own wipe recordings, and 2,000+ itch plays where 30%+ clean the whole shoe and median time passes 3 minutes. If only sneakerheads respond, lean harder into owner stories; if only the before/after gets views and nobody plays past zone one, fix the scrub feel before anything else.
winners.weakestLink: Audience fit and novelty decay. Sneaker-cleaning viewers are not obviously cozy-game buyers, and without real brands sneakerheads may shrug at invented silhouettes, so the owner stories have to do the warming. The cleaning verb also wears off (PowerWash 2's peak was about 13% of the original's), so materials, tools and story chains must keep it fresh, and a generalist restorer adding shoes could take the theme.

provenLoop.note: Cleaning and restoration is one of the most-paid sim loops: PowerWash (17M players), ReStory 500k+, House Flipper 2 1M+, Crime Scene Cleaner 355k in 60 days, CMS2021 ~839k.

openTheme.note: No sneaker restorer exists (confirmed by search), but the cozy-buyer demand is inferred from video views, and generalist restorers (The Repair House, Cozy Game Restoration) could add shoes.

hook.note: A mud-grey shoe and one white stripe is understood in one second with no text.

moment.note: The wipe reveal mirrors a real viral video format shot for shot, and the split shoe with taped name adds a human beat.

feel.note: Three-beat crack/foam/wipe, foam that carries dirt colour, per-material sound, shoe nudge and no pixel hunting; specified to the knob.

click.note: The first wipe lands inside 30 seconds before any menu; the 'keep the mark' choice and owner replies give the deeper click.

look.note: The split shoe with blue tape is legible in a thumbnail, but the product-photo realism sits close to other restoration sims and needs commissioned 3D shoes in several silhouettes.

timing.note: Good window while categories are being claimed, but the restoration wave (Repair House, Cozy Game Restoration, Things Left Unsaid) is closing it.

comeBackAndMoney.note: Overnight sole cure, owner follow-ups and swap-meet reveals give pull, and $14.99 has clear comps, but it is a finite campaign and cleaning novelty decays.

critic.summary: The strongest proven loop in the set, paired with a real-world video format that already gets millions of views and a feel spec that is ready to prototype. It wins if the scrub-then-wipe clip pulls both sneaker and cozy audiences; it dies if only sneakerheads care (no cozy buyers) or if a generalist restorer ships a better shoe level first.
fixesApplied: Merged the two Scuff & Shine drafts: kept the first-person family, the back-room cutting-mat bench, the love-mark tape and zone chords (FP draft) and added the guaranteed first-stroke stripe, circular-scrub bonus, shoe nudge, heart pin and secondary-verb feel (EV draft).
Resolved a contradiction between drafts: the first stroke now only cracks the crust into a pale stripe, so the towel wipe stays the full reveal (three beats instead of two competing payoffs).
Rebuilt the clip so the stripe lands at 1 s, then foam, wipe, taped name, sole timelapse and box photo.
Picked one market plan (spring clips, June Next Fest, back-to-school launch) instead of two conflicting launch windows.
Corrected creator figures to the confirmed 1.6M YouTube / 803K Instagram and dropped the unconfirmed 2.4M TikTok claim; marked the retail shoe-store sims as unconfirmed.
Prove-it test now posts to sneaker AND cozy audiences and requires a response from both, to test the audience-fit risk directly.
Downgraded open theme, look and timing to ok; lowered demand, gap, culture to match calibration (Well Loved is the nearest calibrated comp).

winners.name: Lather & Loaf
winners.hook: Pour three colours blind, drag one swirl, then pull the wire through the loaf and find out what you made.
winners.oneLiner: Run a tiny cold-process soap studio above a Saturday market: tint batter, pour layers and drag a swirl stick through a wooden mould, let it cure, then pull the wire cutter through the loaf. Every bar is a new cross-section of your own pour, and the best ones fill customers' order cards.

clipStoryboard.shot: Overhead on a walnut mould of cream batter. Three enamel jugs (rose, teal, gold) tip in from height and fold into ribbons. Heard: a thick, slow glug and a bench creak. (This is the half that mobile soap-cutting ads never show.)
A bamboo stick drags one figure-eight; the surface feathers into a peacock pattern. Heard: a soft wet drag.
Hard cut: the cured loaf on the cutter bed in morning light, its top now plain and matte, giving nothing away. A brass latch clacks; the lever is gripped.
The lever comes down; the wire bows as it sinks through with a crisp crunch-squeak and a wooden 'tock'. The bar clings for a beat, peels away and tips onto its side.
Hold on the wet, glossy cut face: a teal heart sits inside a rose spiral nobody could see from the top. The camera eases in; the sheen dries to matte.
Two more pulls in rhythm, then ten bars fanned out on kraft paper like a flipbook, the heart morphing bar to bar. Heard: one low nylon-guitar note.

provenLoop.loop: Take an order, craft it with hands-on real-world steps, get a reveal you made yourself, sell it, buy new materials and techniques (Dressmaker's craft-to-order loop plus the TCG-style reveal, ten reveals per loaf).

openTheme.demand: Soap cutting is one of the oldest 'oddly satisfying' formats: soap-cutting videos had about 1.5B TikTok views and #soapcutting 934k+ Instagram posts by a 2022 press count (the 3.6B figure in the draft could not be confirmed and is dropped; follower counts for individual soap makers are unverified). Mobile 'Soap Cutting' toys are still being updated in 2026, so people play it, though for free. Dressmaker shows the hand-craft crowd buys on Steam right now, and the research names candle and soap making as open Dressmaker-adjacent themes. Paid demand for a soap game is inferred, not measured.
openTheme.supply: No soap- or candle-making sim on Steam (confirmed again by search). Competitors are mobile ASMR toys (Soap Cutting, Soap Cutting Relax, Idle Soap ASMR), a Sims 4 soap mod and a soap-shop mobile project in development (Bunno's Soap Shop, a university project). They are weak because you only cut prefab bars: you never make the soap, so the reveal is not yours and there is no craft or shop. The danger is perceptual, not competitive: millions of people have seen soap cutting in mobile ads, so the clip must show the pour. A cautionary craft comp: Master of Pottery (Steam, pottery wheel plus showroom, $5.99) has only ~538 reviews at 97% after years in Early Access, so a pleasant craft bench without a viral reveal stays small.
openTheme.searched: Searched 'soap making simulator Steam cold process soap cutting', 'soap making simulator Steam game 2026', '"soap shop simulator" OR "candle shop simulator" Steam', 'soap cutting TikTok views billion' and 'Master of Pottery Steam'. Found only mobile cutting toys, a Sims mod, a mobile project in development and no Steam soap studio; the name is free.

coreAction.verb: Slice the loaf (pull the wire cutter)
coreAction.input: Mouse: grab the cutter lever and drag down; lever depth follows the cursor 1:1. Controller: right trigger is analog lever depth (full pull = through the loaf). Touch: drag down anywhere on the right half of the screen. A scroll tick or bumper ratchets the loaf forward one bar-width.
coreAction.response: Within one frame the lever rotates with your drag. The first ~8% of travel is free play, then the wire meets the top skin with a sprung 'clack', bows into a shallow curve and leaves a thin indent line along the top. A dry 'tick' plays at contact. From there the wire's depth tracks your drag against a firmness curve, so you feel the soap pushing back.
feedback: Anticipation: free travel before contact, a sprung clack at contact, and a 4% camera ease-in, so the cut always 'loads' before it bites.
Wire bow: the wire bends up to ~6 mm (visual) in proportion to pull speed and the loaf's firmness, and straightens when you ease off. This shows resistance without any UI.

Surface deformation: the top skin dimples along the wire and a bead of glycerin 'sweat' squeezes out along the cut line (decal plus 3-8 crumb particles at the wire's exit point; embeds like lavender buds occasionally pop out).

Sound, layered: (a) a granular crunch whose grains fire every 1.5-3 mm of travel, pitch tracking speed ±15%; (b) randomized squeak transients from a 6-sample pool, ±8% pitch; (c) a faint wire 'string' tone that rises as tension builds; (d) a wooden 'tock' when the wire hits the bed; (e) a soft thump as the bar tips, volume and pitch set by bar weight. All of it is close-mic foley of real soap cut on a real cutter.

Follow-through: the two halves cling for 60-120 ms (a sticky separation), then the bar peels away and tips onto its side as a rigid body with 2-3% squash on landing, then recovers. It is soap, so it has a little give.
Light: the fresh cut face has a wet specular sheen that dries to matte over ~2 s, which sells 'just cut' in every frame of a clip.

Camera: no shake (it is cozy). A 1-frame micro-bump on the 'tock', then on the tip-over the camera holds 0.4 s, pushes in ~6% and turns ~3° toward the cut face. It releases when you touch the lever again.

Rhythm and the pour (the other half of the hands' time): after three bars each full pull auto-ratchets the loaf one notch with a click, so slicing becomes pull-click-pull-click. The pour is just as physical: jug tilt follows your drag angle 1:1, the batter stream thickens with tilt, folds into ribbons where it lands (written into the 3D colour field), and the glug pitch drops as the jug empties.
Haptics: on a controller, a low rumble textured per crunch grain and one firm pulse on the 'tock'; on phones, light taps per grain cluster.
UI: nothing during the cut. After the bar lands, a small kraft tag slides in naming the pattern ('Peacock, lopsided') only if an order asked for one; otherwise the bar just joins the row.
coreAction.payoff: The bar tips and a pattern no one has seen turns toward the light. Because the swirl is a real 3D volume, every slice is another cross-section, so a loaf is ten reveals that morph bar to bar like a flipbook. Rare emergent shapes (a heart, a clean spiral, a 'galaxy') earn a soft chime and a named entry in the pattern journal.
tuning: Free travel before contact (5-12% of lever travel): more makes the bite feel heavier.
Wire bow max (3-8 mm) and spring constant: the main 'resistance' read.
Firmness curve per recipe and cure stage: young soap is soft and squishy, fully cured is crisp and crunchy.
Crunch grain spacing (1.5-3 mm) and pitch range (±8-15%): crispness versus mush.
Clinging separation delay (60-120 ms) and tip torque: how 'fresh' and heavy a bar feels.
Landing squash (2-4%) and recovery damping.
Camera push-in (4-8%), turn (2-5°) and hold (0.3-0.6 s).
Wet-sheen fade time (1.5-3 s).
Jerk threshold for cosmetic chatter marks on the cut face.
Volume resolution of the swirl field (e.g. 64×32×128 voxels): sharper patterns versus WebGL cost.
Pour stream width per degree of jug tilt and ribbon fold strength: how readable your own pour is when it reappears in the cut face.
feelsBadIf: The wire moves at a canned animation speed whatever you do. Fix: depth is always driven by your input against the firmness curve.
The inside pattern doesn't match what you poured (a pre-baked texture). Fix: the pour and swirl write into a real 3D colour field that the cut samples, so players recognise their own pour.
The crunch loops audibly. Fix: granular grains, a sample pool and speed-tracked pitch.
A bad cut wastes the loaf. Fix: mistakes are only cosmetic (chatter marks, a crooked edge); uneven bars sell as cheap 'seconds' or get grated into confetti soap, so nothing is lost.
Ten bars per loaf feels like a chore. Fix: the ratchet rhythm after bar three, plus each bar being a new reveal.
Input lag in the browser. Fix: read raw pointer events and apply at most one frame of smoothing.
The bar falls like a brick. Fix: clinging separation, squash and the wet sheen.
The pour is a menu choice (pick a 'swirl type' button). Fix: every pour and swirl is a hand gesture whose exact path shows up inside the loaf, so the reveal is always yours.
The clip looks like a mobile soap-cutting ad. Fix: every marketing clip opens on the pour and the plain top, so the slice is a reveal of something made, not a prefab bar.

clickMoment.first: In the first minute you tip three jugs into the mould (you can only see the top), drag the stick once, watch a cozy dusk-to-dawn timelapse, then pull the lever. The first bar tips over and the inside looks nothing like the top. It is your pour, folded in ways you didn't predict. The second pull shows a different cross-section, and it clicks: every slice is a new reveal of something you made.
clickMoment.deeper: The deeper click is learning to pour blind on purpose. You read 'trace' (thin batter swirls, thick batter holds layers), choose drop, hanger or in-the-pot swirls and embeds, and start predicting what bar 5 will look like. The mastery beat is a wedding order that asks for a heart hidden in the middle bar, and you land it. Attachment comes from naming your signature recipe and seeing regulars at the stall ask for it again.

look.short: Sunny attic soap studio · pastel bars on oiled walnut · kraft paper and string
look.vibe: A small whitewashed attic room with a slanted skylight. Morning light falls across an oiled walnut bench, a wooden mould, enamel jugs with drips down their sides and a brass-and-steel wire cutter. The soap is the colour: chalky pastel batter that turns glossy where it is freshly cut. Everything else is warm wood, linen, kraft paper and twine, slightly soft-focused, like a handmade-goods Instagram account with real dust in the air.
look.signature: The 'flipbook row': ten freshly cut bars fanned out side by side, the swirl visibly morphing from bar to bar, each with a wet sheen on its cut face. You recognise it in a thumbnail the way you recognise a sliced cake.
references: Dressmaker's warm boutique close-ups
real cold-process soap-maker videos (overhead pour shots and cutter close-ups)
Unpacking's tactile object love
A Little to the Left's clean, calm framing
Kinfolk-style handmade-goods photography
avoid: Neon 'satisfying' mobile-ad colours and glitter overload
Hyper-real PBR plastic sheen that makes soap look like candy
UI meters and percentages over the bench

winners.sound: ASMR-first: every cut, pour and drag is close-mic foley recorded on real soap (a real wire cutter and loaf are cheap to buy, and recording them is devlog content). Music is sparse nylon guitar and a soft Rhodes that drop out whenever your hand is on the lever, so the crunch carries the moment. Market days add distant chatter and a church bell.

timing.session: A studio day runs about 10-15 minutes: read 2-3 order cards, pour one or two loaves (2-4 minutes each), slice and bevel the loaf that cured overnight (about 2 minutes of pure rhythm), then stamp, wrap and shelve. Every third day is the Saturday stall, where you price bars and meet regulars. The longer arc is unlocking techniques, scents and moulds and filling the 40-pattern journal.
timing.firstMinute: No menus: a loaf mould and three pre-tinted jugs. Pour (15 s), one swirl drag (5 s), a cure timelapse (5 s), then the first three slices with the reveal on each. The first order card arrives only after the third bar has tipped.
timing.marketWindow: Dressmaker (Sept 21 2026) and ReStory (Aug 2026) just proved tactile craft and restoration breakouts, and the research expects Dressmaker clones to target sewing and knitting first, which leaves soap open. Cozy releases jumped from 632 in 2025 to 1,041 by late Sept 2026, so a sharp reveal is needed to stand out. Handmade soap is a classic gift: reveal the Steam page with a 'holiday soap' clip in the gifting season, put the demo in a Steam Next Fest, pitch Wholesome Direct, and launch 1.0 in early November so holiday gifting and Steam's Autumn and Winter sales follow.

comeBack.short: The loaf you poured yesterday has cured and is waiting on the cutter, so the reveal is literally banked for your next session.
comeBack.long: A pattern journal with 40 named swirls (some rare and emergent), technique unlocks (embeds, mica lines, rimmed tops, salt bars), regulars whose orders build on past ones, seasonal scents and colour drops, stall decoration, and shareable pour codes: send a friend your recipe and they slice 'your' loaf in their game, so their reveal matches yours.

money.model: Premium on Steam, after a free browser toy and a paid itch.io/Ko-fi supporter build; small seasonal DLC scent-and-mould packs later.
money.evidence: Dressmaker launched at $14.99 and recouped in under 24h; Potion Craft sold 100k in 3 days (confirmed); implied average realised prices in the genre are $10–12 (Supermarket Simulator, TCG Card Shop). Well-reviewed themed sims without a breakout land at 25k–120k copies (Bookshop Simulator ~50.9k / $488k, Tavern Manager ~92.3k / $830k); sims with no clip-able hook land under 10k (Piece by Piece ~4.8k, low confidence), and a pleasant craft bench at $5.99 (Master of Pottery, ~538 reviews) stays small, which is why the reveal must be proven first. Cozy games that reach 1,000 reviews correspond to roughly $150k gross.

winners.proveItFirst: Build a one-screen browser toy (Three.js, WebGL2 3D texture): one mould, three jugs, one swirl stick, a cure timelapse and the cutter. No shop, no menus. Before posting, check that a real soap maker cannot tell your cut face from a photo of real cold-process soap at phone size. Post 5 different 7–10 second clips of real player-made pours (always opening on the pour, no text) to TikTok and Shorts, and link the toy on itch.io with a 'follow for the game' button. A yes is any clip above 100k views with 'what game is this' comments and fewer than about 1 in 10 top comments calling it 'one of those mobile ads', or 2,000+ itch plays where the median player pours 3+ loaves and 5%+ click through to follow or wishlist. A no is players slicing one loaf and leaving.
winners.weakestLink: Perceived depth and the mobile-ad shadow. Free soap-cutting toys have trained people to see soap slicing as a 30-second ad, so the clip must sell the pour and the Steam game must prove the craft (trace, techniques, hidden-pattern orders) is worth $15; the shop side is the thinnest part of the design. Master of Pottery shows a well-liked craft bench can stay tiny. The 3D swirl volume must also look like real soap, or the reveal becomes a gimmick.

provenLoop.note: Craft-to-order with a reveal sold for Potion Craft (100k in 3 days) and Dressmaker (400k+ wishlists), but Dressmaker's final sales are not in yet and a craft bench without a viral reveal (Master of Pottery) stays small.

openTheme.note: Confirmed empty on Steam: only mobile prefab-cutting toys, a Sims mod and a mobile project; soap cutting has 1.5B+ TikTok views.

hook.note: 'Pour blind, slice to find out' is instant, but a stranger may read any soap-slicing clip as a mobile ad; the clip has to open on the pour to separate itself.

moment.note: The bar tipping to show a hidden heart you poured is a proven satisfying beat made personal, and every loaf yields ten.

feel.note: Analog lever against a firmness curve, wire bow, granular crunch, clinging separation and wet sheen, plus a 1:1 hand pour; mistakes are cosmetic.

click.note: The first bar reveals inside the first minute; the deeper click is pouring blind on purpose and landing a hidden-heart order.

look.note: The flipbook row of freshly cut bars is a thumbnail people already recognise; one bench suits commissioned and bought art.

timing.note: Gifting season and the post-Dressmaker moment help, but cozy supply is up 143% and craft clones are coming.

comeBackAndMoney.note: The overnight cure banks the next reveal and $14.99 has comps, but depth beyond the slice is unproven and the ceiling is mid-tier unless the clip spreads.

critic.summary: The emptiest theme in the set with the cheapest bench to build, and a reveal that is literally the player's own work, ten times per loaf. It wins if clips that open on the pour read as 'a game where you make it' rather than another mobile soap ad; it dies if the 3D swirl doesn't look like real soap or if players slice one loaf and see nothing deeper to buy.

winners.name: Well Loved
winners.theme: Small-object restoration with nostalgia: plush and toy hospital
winners.hook: Close a split seam in one pull and watch a 30-year-old bear plump back to life.
winners.oneLiner: Run a tiny plush hospital: admit worn, much-loved toys with their owners' notes, wash and fluff them, restuff and ladder-stitch their seams shut, mend eyes and noses without erasing the love marks, and sometimes fix an old voice box and hear what it says.

clipStoryboard.shot: Close-up: a balding honey-coloured bear on a felt-topped bench under a gooseneck lamp, a split side seam with stuffing poking out, a brown paper hospital tag on its wrist. Heard: a soft lamp click.
A curved needle stabs left, right, left, right across the gap; loose thread loops form a little ladder. Heard: a soft tick on each stab and a thread whisper.
A hand pulls the thread: the ladder rungs tighten one after another, the edges roll in and the seam vanishes. Heard: an ascending music-box run, one note per rung.
The bear plumps up with a little bounce; one ear flops; its button eye catches the lamp.
The bear sits beside an old photo of a toddler hugging it; a tiny voice box under the bench clicks and a crackly recorded voice says 'night night'. Then the hospital tag gets a 'discharged' stamp.

coreAction.verb: Ladder-stitch and cinch (stab left, stab right, then one pull closes the seam)
coreAction.input: Mouse: the needle follows the cursor; swing it back and forth across the seam in a zig-zag and each crossing onto the far bank snaps a stitch in (no dots to click). Hold and drag away from the seam to cinch. Controller: left and right triggers stab the left and right banks in an alternating walking rhythm, right stick pulls the thread. Touch: zig-zag a finger across the seam, then drag away to cinch.
coreAction.response: Within 50 ms of the needle crossing onto a bank, its tip pushes into the fabric, the fabric dimples around it (vertex displacement), and it pops through with a few fibre motes. Faint chalk marks show the ideal spacing, but the stitch lands where you actually crossed. The thread follows as a rope that lies as a loose rung across the gap, so after each zig-zag pair you can count your ladder growing, at your own tempo.
feedback: Anticipation: the needle hovers and its tip glints over the next valid dot; the fabric pre-dimples slightly as it approaches.
Stab: a 40 ms push-in with fabric dimple, then a pop-through with 2-4 fibre motes and a soft 'tick' (6 sample variations, ±6% pitch).
Thread: verlet rope with a slight overshoot; pulling through plays a cotton 'fffp' whose pitch follows pull speed.
Ladder rungs: loose loops visibly cross the gap, a physical progress bar with no UI.

The cinch: on the pull, rungs tighten in sequence with a 30-50 ms stagger, each one playing the next note of an ascending pentatonic music-box run; the fabric edges roll inward and meet, and the seam disappears.
Plump: the limb or body inflates 4-8% with spring overshoot (damping ~0.5) and a soft 'fwump'; ears and loose limbs get secondary wobble.
Camera: a slow 5% push-in during the cinch that releases on the plump; no shake. On a finished patient, the camera rests on the eyes as one catches the lamp.
Fur: brushing a matted patch with a slicker brush combs shell-textured fur from flat and clumped to soft and lifted, a small PowerWash-style reveal on plush.
Haptics: a crisp click per stab and a rising buzz through the cinch, peaking on the plump.
UI: almost none. Spacing guides are faint chalk dots; uneven stitching shows physically as a slightly puckered seam that the owner notices kindly rather than as a score.
coreAction.payoff: One long pull turns a ragged split into an invisible seam with a little melody, and the toy plumps up and 'looks back' at you. On some patients, a repaired voice box plays a decades-old recording made for the child who owned it.
tuning: Rung tighten stagger (30-50 ms) and the note scale: the musicality of the cinch.
Plump amount (4-8%), spring stiffness and overshoot.
Fabric dimple depth and radius per material (felt, mohair, minky, velour).
Needle push-in duration (30-60 ms) and pop-through particle count.
Dot spacing tolerance: how forgiving placement is before a seam puckers.
Cinch drag distance required (short feels cheap, long feels like work).
Fur shell count and comb radius for the de-matting pass.
Camera push-in (3-6%) and release timing.
Zig-zag crossing tolerance and stitch snap distance: how freely the hand can swing before stitches go uneven.
feelsBadIf: Free-form cloth simulation tangles or clips. Fix: seams are authored paths per plush, so the stitch is always physically clean while still under your control.

Stitching becomes clicking dots at a chore pace (the most-repeated action turning into a QTE). Fix: a continuous zig-zag gesture with stitches landing where you cross, short seams of 6–10 stitches, and the cinch payoff after every seam.
The cinch is a canned animation. Fix: rungs only tighten as far as you have pulled, so a slow pull plays the melody slowly.
The toys look like stiff plastic. Fix: commissioned hero plush with real fabric textures, fur shells and soft-body squash on every touch; this is the art budget's main line.
Perfectionism gets punished. Fix: small imperfections become 'love marks' the owner appreciates, and only skipping a step fails a job.
It reads as a kids' game. Fix: adult owners and adult stories (a bear that went through chemo with someone, a rabbit from a late father), muted storybook tones rather than candy colours.

The plush look stiff in the browser. Fix: prove one commissioned hero bear with shell-texture fur and soft-body squash in WebGL before any other content; if it doesn't read as soft at phone size, the project stops there.

clickMoment.first: In the first minute you take a bear with a split seam, tap left-right-left-right to lay six rungs, then pull: the rungs zip shut with a rising melody and the bear plumps up in your hands. That 'one pull and it's whole again' is the click, before any note or menu.
clickMoment.deeper: The deeper click comes when you start choosing what not to fix: you leave the worn nose a child rubbed for 20 years, re-use the original button eye found in the stuffing, and tape the owner's name tag back on. Attachment lands with the first voice box: you fix the tiny mechanism, press the paw and hear a grandmother's recorded goodnight, then read the owner's letter. Later, an unclaimed stray on the 'adopt' shelf becomes yours to restore and keep.

look.short: Warm storybook toy hospital · felt-topped bench under a gooseneck lamp · honey, cream and rose
look.vibe: A small upstairs workroom like a cross between a tailor's and a children's ward: a sage-green felt bench, a gooseneck lamp, jars of buttons and glass eyes, a washing line of drying patients over the radiator, and paper hospital tags on every toy. The plush are rendered with real softness: mohair pile, worn bald patches, faded velour, slightly uneven stitching. Light is warm lamp-glow against blue evening windows, quiet and tender rather than cute.
look.signature: The brown paper hospital tag tied on a string around every patient's wrist, with a handwritten name and ailment ('Biscuit, 31, split seam, missing eye') and a little plaster on the toy.
references: Real toy-hospital photography (Tokyo and Singapore soft toy hospitals)
Dressmaker's tactile sewing close-ups
Unpacking's object-story intimacy
The Velveteen Rabbit illustrations
Jellycat product photography for fabric softness
avoid: Glossy plastic toys or rubbery fur

winners.sound: Soft cotton and felt foley, needle ticks, thread whispers and the 'fwump' of a plumped limb, with every cinch playing an ascending run on a music box so the shop literally sounds like mending. Music is a gentle felt piano and celesta. Old voice boxes are the sonic signature: short, crackly human-recorded messages (lullabies, 'I love you', a child's laugh) recorded by real voice actors.

timing.session: One patient takes about 8-12 minutes: admission (read the note, tie the tag), triage (squeeze to find lumps, check seams and eyes, find what is hidden in the stuffing), wash, dry overnight on the radiator line, then stitch, restuff, mend eyes and nose, fluff the fur and discharge with a photo against the window. A day is 2-3 patients, with yesterday's washed patients waiting dry and fluffy. The arc is harder cases (antique mohair, voice boxes, jointed bears), owner story chains and the adopt shelf.
timing.firstMinute: A bear is already on the bench with its seam split. Six taps and one pull close it with the melody and the plump. Only then does the box's note get read: 'This is Biscuit. He's older than me. Please don't make him new.' The love-mark idea is introduced right there.
timing.marketWindow: Dressmaker (Sept 21 2026) has just put sewing in front of hundreds of thousands of players and the kidult plush boom (Jellycat +66%) is at its height, but sewing is where Dressmaker clones will land first, so the clip must be out before them. Best moments: a Steam page reveal with a 'tell me about your childhood plush' call for stories, a demo in Steam Next Fest, a Wholesome Direct pitch, and 1.0 in early November ahead of holiday gifting, with a real toy-hospital charity tie-in for press.

comeBack.short: Yesterday's washed patients are dry on the radiator line and waiting to be stitched, and an owner's reply letter with a photo has arrived.
comeBack.long: A wall of discharge photos and letters, a library of recovered voice-box messages, the adopt shelf of unclaimed strays to restore and keep, harder materials and antique techniques, recurring families whose toys come back across generations, and seasonal events like a winter toy drive.

money.model: Premium on Steam after a free browser toy and a paid supporter build; later DLC patient packs and console ports (Switch suits it).
money.evidence: Dressmaker at $14.99 recouped in under 24h; Unpacking (~$20) sold 1M+ and ported widely; genre implied average realised price $10–12; 45.2% of cozy games at $20+ reach 1,000 reviews (budget confound). Downside comp: Piece by Piece (cozy repair, strong publisher) ~4.8k copies (low confidence) without a clip moment, which is exactly what the cinch has to fix. Themed-sim mid-tier band is 25k–120k copies.

winners.proveItFirst: First, commission one hero bear and get it soft in WebGL (shell fur, squash on touch); if it doesn't read as plush at phone size, stop. Then build a browser toy with that bear, one split seam and one matted patch: zig-zag, cinch, plump, brush. No shop. Post 6–8 second cinch clips to TikTok and Shorts with no text, plus one asking viewers to describe their childhood plush. A yes is a clip above 100k views or a save rate above 3%, 200+ comments telling their own plush stories, or 2,000+ itch plays where 40%+ of players finish the bear. A no is views without stories and players leaving before the cinch.
winners.weakestLink: Proof of audience and art cost. Piece by Piece, the closest cozy repair game, sold ~4.8k with a good publisher, so the theme alone will not sell; everything rides on the cinch clip spreading. Plush also needs high-quality commissioned fabric and fur art (Exotica 2's weak animals sank it to 78%), which is the biggest spend and the hardest part to get right for a solo creator.

provenLoop.note: Restore-with-story is ReStory's loop (500k+), sewing is Dressmaker's verb, objects-as-story is Unpacking's (1M+).

openTheme.note: No adult plush hospital on Steam and kidult demand is confirmed (Jellycat +66%), but the closest cozy repair game (Piece by Piece) sold small and sewing clones are coming.

hook.note: A split bear closing in one pull and plumping up needs no text.

moment.note: The ladder-stitch cinch is already a popular real sewing clip; the voice-box message is a second, emotional beat.

feel.note: The cinch and plump are excellent on paper and stitching is now a free zig-zag, but everything rides on fabric and fur reading as soft in a browser, the hardest art-tech problem in the set.

click.note: The cinch lands within the first minute; choosing what not to fix and the voice box give the deeper click.

look.note: The brown paper hospital tag on every patient is a distinct thumbnail signature with a tender, non-kiddie palette.

timing.note: Holiday toy season and the plush boom line up, but sewing is exactly where post-Dressmaker clones will land.

comeBackAndMoney.note: Overnight drying line, letters and the adopt shelf give pull; premium comps are clear but the nearest downside comp is close.

critic.summary: The most emotional idea in the set, with a cinch that is a real viral sewing beat and a theme riding a confirmed adult-plush boom. It wins if one commissioned bear looks genuinely soft in the browser and the cinch clip pulls people's own plush stories; it dies on art cost or if it reads as a Piece by Piece-style generic repair game.

winners.name: Dondurma Days
winners.hook: You're the Turkish ice-cream man: tease every customer with the cone, and hand it over at the exact moment they laugh.
winners.oneLiner: Run a dondurma cart at a summer evening bazaar. Stretch the chewy ice cream on a long brass paddle, then flip, dodge and snatch the cone back from each customer, and hand it over at their peak laugh (before they storm off) for the biggest tip. Stack bigger multi-scoop orders that must stay stuck through your tricks, discover each regular's favourite trick, and spend tips on flavours, new tricks, a bigger cart and new bazaars.

clipStoryboard.shot: Side view of a turquoise-tiled cart at dusk. A small girl on tiptoe reaches for a cone held out on a metre-long brass paddle. One bright brass-bell DING.
Her fingers close, the paddle flicks, and the cone spins upside down. The ice cream stays stuck on as a stretchy white ribbon. She's holding an empty cone. Whoosh, then a rubbery squeak.
The paddle taps the cone on her nose. She giggles, and the queue behind her starts laughing, one person and then three.
She reaches again. This time the cone settles into her hand. A 100 ms freeze-frame, then the whole queue cheers and coins arc into a brass tip jar with rising clinks.
A small instant photo of her face, beaming and smeared with pistachio, slides into the corner and pins itself to the cart.
