coreAction.verb: Tease (flick, dodge and snatch the cone on a long paddle, then hand it over at the laugh peak)
coreAction.input: One finger or the mouse. Drag to move the paddle tip, flick fast to flip the cone, lift your finger near the customer's open hand to hand it over. Controller: left stick moves the paddle, flick the right stick to flip, A to hand over. The cone always sits about 80 px above the finger so your thumb never hides it.
coreAction.response: Within one frame the paddle tip springs toward your finger. It's slightly underdamped, so it overshoots by about 6% and settles in about 90 ms. The white dondurma ribbon between scoop and cone stretches and swings with the paddle. The customer's eyes follow the cone at once, and their hand starts a visible pull-back 'tell' before each lunge.
feedback: Animation: the cone squashes up to 1.2x along the direction of travel on hard reversals and springs back. The dondurma is an 8-segment verlet rope that stretches like taffy and snaps back with a wobble. A flip spins the cone 540° with ease-out and a small overshoot.
Anticipation: every customer lunge has a 120–200 ms tell (shoulders up, hand drawn back, tongue out for kids). Dodges are about reading people, not luck.

Faces as the meter: there's no bar, only the face and body. Giggle, laugh, belly laugh, then a smirk, a frown and arms crossed. Kids bounce, grandpas wag a finger, tourists lift a phone. A tiny laugh bubble inflates above the head for readability on small screens.

Sound: the paddle taps a brass bell, and each tease in a chain steps up the scale (do-re-mi-fa). The flick whoosh is pitched by flick speed. The ribbon makes a rubbery squeak-thwop. Kid giggles are randomised ±3 semitones so no two match. A crowd-laugh layer grows with the combo, from one voice to the whole queue.
Hitstop: 80 ms freeze on a perfect last-instant dodge and 100 ms on the handover, with a 3% camera push-in on the customer's face.
Particles: sprinkles of crushed pistachio fly off on flips. On handover, coins burst out patterned like Iznik tiles. On a frustrated customer, a single cartoon sweat drop.
Physical tip jar: coins are rigid bodies that drop into a brass jar on the cart, and the clinks rise in pitch as the jar fills. No number flies to a HUD corner.
Haptics: 10 ms pulse on each dodge and 30 ms on handover (navigator.vibrate on Android, controller rumble on Steam).
Crowd follow-through: after a great handover the next two people in the queue applaud and lean forward, so the next tease starts with an audience.
Photo: the best reaction of the evening is saved as an instant photo pinned to the cart. It's shareable and doubles as the collection.
coreAction.payoff: The handover at the laugh peak: freeze, the customer's hand closes, the queue erupts, coins rain into the brass jar, and their beaming face is pinned to your cart. Wait one beat too long and they storm off. Hand it over one beat early and you get a polite smile and a small tip.
tuning: Paddle spring stiffness and damping: how 'held' versus 'floaty' the paddle feels (aim for under 90 ms settle)
Tell duration per customer type (120–200 ms): how readable the lunges are
Lunge speed and reach radius: how hard a dodge is
Laugh curve per customer type (kids tolerate long teases, grandpas short ones but tip big, filming tourists reward longer routines): how much there is to read
Laugh-peak window width (start about 400 ms, narrows with fame): how hard the handover timing is
Flick velocity threshold for a flip: accidental versus deliberate tricks
Hitstop length (60–120 ms): how much each success weighs
Tip multiplier per extra trick and per audience size: risk versus reward
Customers per evening and queue patience: the pace of a session
Scoop stack stickiness and wobble (1–4 scoops): bigger orders make every flip riskier and every handover worth more.
Combo memory: how many different tricks a routine needs before the crowd multiplier grows, so repeating one flip stops paying.
feelsBadIf: Grabs feel random. Always show the tell, and never let a lunge land inside it.
The paddle lags or swims. If settle time goes over about 100 ms it feels like dragging through syrup.
Your thumb covers the cone on a phone. Keep the cone offset above the finger.
The laugh peak can't be read. If players need a meter, the faces have failed, so redraw them bigger and simpler.

Failure is humiliating or punishing. Storm-offs are comic (a huff, a stomp), the customer comes back next evening for a 'rematch' with a bigger tip, and no customer is ever mocked. They are in on the game.
Every customer plays the same. Each type needs a different laugh curve and tell, or it turns into a one-trick toy.
The culture reads as a gag. Vendor, music and bazaar are drawn and checked with Turkish collaborators.

clickMoment.first: About 15 seconds in, the first kid reaches, you flick almost by accident, the cone flips upside down, she's left holding an empty cone, and the queue laughs. Then you hand it over while she's giggling, coins pour in, and you realise this isn't a cooking game: you're performing, and the timing is yours.
clickMoment.deeper: A few evenings in you start reading people: Dede Ahmet only laughs at the nose-tap, the tourist filming you wants a three-trick routine, the shy kid needs one quick flip and an early handover. Each regular has a secret favourite trick you discover by watching their face, written into a little notebook. Your first chained routine on a wobbling three-scoop order draws a semicircle of onlookers and the tip jar overflows; later the photo wall of regulars' faces is the thing you're attached to.

look.short: Golden-hour bazaar cart · hand-painted 2D side view · turquoise tiles, brass and a metre of stretchy white ice cream
look.vibe: A single side-on view of a small cart with a hand-painted Iznik-tile front, a brass bell and copper lids, at the warm end of a summer evening. Behind it, a soft-focus bazaar of string lights, a ferry horn far off, and silhouettes strolling past. Customers are chunky, expressive gouache characters with big readable faces and hands, a little like animated storybook illustrations. Everything is still except the paddle, the ribbon of ice cream and the faces, which are where your eye should be.
look.signature: A metre-long ribbon of glossy white dondurma stretched between the brass paddle and the tub, hanging in a perfect arc over a child's reaching hand
references: Good Pizza, Great Pizza (single-counter readability)
Iznik tilework and Ottoman miniature colour, simplified
Gouache children's-book illustration (big faces, big hands)
Real Kahramanmaraş-style dondurma vendor videos (the choreography, not the costume gag)
avoid: A visible patience bar that steals focus from faces
Busy backgrounds that compete with the paddle

winners.sound: Bright and handmade. The brass bell is the lead instrument: every tease plays a note, so a good routine literally plays a melody. Under it, a light darbuka and oud loop commissioned from a Turkish musician, which drops out for a beat at each hitstop. Crowd laughter is the dynamic layer: an empty street at the start of the evening, a laughing crowd by the end.

timing.session: Each customer takes 8–20 seconds of tease and handover. An evening is 12–20 customers as dusk turns to night and the crowd thickens, ending in a 'last cone' finale and a look at the evening's photo. Between evenings you take one quick upgrade decision (a flavour, a trick, a cart part). On Steam, a summer season strings evenings across three bazaars (hometown square, ferry pier, seaside promenade) and ends in a festival night.
timing.firstMinute: No menu. The cart is open and a kid is already in the queue. One ghosted finger shows 'drag'. The first flick happens almost by accident, the queue laughs, the first handover pays out, and a second customer (a grandpa with a much shorter fuse) teaches you that people differ. All before 60 seconds.
timing.marketWindow: Dondurma vendor clips peak with summer tourist season, so post the browser slice and clips as northern-hemisphere summer begins. Bring a Steam demo to the June Steam Next Fest so the summer bazaar theme matches the season, and launch on Steam the following early summer. The format is native to vertical video, which is where the real-world vendor clips already circulate.

comeBack.short: Tonight's grudge customer wants a rematch, a regular's favourite trick is still undiscovered in your notebook, and a new trick or flavour from last evening is waiting to try on the queue.
comeBack.long: A cast of regulars with their own tells, favourite tricks and small stories that move forward each evening, a photo wall you fill with reactions, routines composed from unlocked tricks (nose-tap, cone-swap, behind-the-back, the triple-scoop spin), multi-scoop orders that raise the stakes, a nightly 'festival crowd' on the web version where the same seeded queue lets friends compare tips, and new bazaars with different crowds.

money.model: Free browser version on Poki/CrazyGames (ad revenue share), then a premium Steam version with the full season and regulars' stories, then mobile if it sells
money.evidence: GPGP earns 60% ads / 40% IAP on 300M+ downloads and also sells on Steam. Poki pays 100% of ad revenue on traffic you bring and 50/50 on theirs, with 100M monthly players, but its curation is selective. Kebab Chefs made 242.8k copies / $3.5M at about $15. Fluffy Onsen shows a cheap, focused game can move volume (tracker estimates range from ~61.7k copies / $314k to ~188k / $814k). Cozy games under $5 hit 1,000 reviews only 2.7% of the time, which is why the Steam version is priced above that; no single-verb counter toy in the research has sold at Steam scale, so the Steam version is the uncertain part.

winners.proveItFirst: Build one screen: the cart, one paddle and three customer types with commissioned placeholder faces. Record two 8-second vertical clips (an 'empty cone' fail and a perfect handover) and post them on TikTok/Shorts with the playable itch.io link pinned. A yes is any clip passing about 50k views with comments asking where to play, plus itch players whose median session runs past 5 minutes (not 3: depth is the question) with at least a third coming back for a second evening. Also show the slice to two or three Turkish players before posting; if the portrayal reads as a gag to them, fix it first. If the clip gets views but the slice doesn't hold people, tune tells and the peak window before building anything else.
winners.weakestLink: Depth. A single tease verb might be a 10-minute toy rather than a season-long game, and the Steam version only works if customer-reading and routine-building keep revealing new layers. A close second risk is cultural portrayal: it needs Turkish collaborators to be warm rather than a novelty.

provenLoop.note: The single-counter serve-and-tip loop is GPGP's (300M+), with Kebab Chefs and Coffee Talk as premium proof, but the tease-timing verb itself has never sold.

openTheme.note: Searches found only an unrated iPad toy, an interactive fiction and generic ice-cream makers; nobody owns the tease.

hook.note: The real vendor trick is already a recurring viral video, so the hook explains itself with no words.

moment.note: The empty-cone flip and the handover at peak laugh are clips by design.

feel.note: Spring paddle with 90 ms settle, verlet ribbon, readable 120–200 ms tells, hitstop, a bell scale and a physical tip jar make it skill-based and physical.

click.note: The first laugh lands within 15 seconds; reading regulars' favourite tricks is the deeper click.

look.note: Distinctive gouache-and-Iznik direction, but it depends on a strong character illustrator and careful cultural art direction.

timing.note: Short customer loops and a summer launch matched to vendor-clip season, but there is no rising trend behind it, only a perennial meme.

comeBackAndMoney.note: Rematches, favourite tricks and multi-scoop orders help on paper, but a one-verb toy may be done in an evening, and portal ad income plus an $8 Steam version has no direct comp in the research.

critic.summary: The cheapest, fastest test in the set, with a hook the real world already made viral and a feel spec that rewards skill. It can win as a web hit that graduates to a small Steam game, but it dies if the tease is a ten-minute toy with no depth, or if the cultural portrayal reads as a novelty gag.
fixesApplied: Added depth systems to the design itself: multi-scoop orders that must stay stuck through tricks, each regular's secret favourite trick, combo memory so repeating one flip stops paying, and a seeded nightly crowd for the web version.
Raised the prove-it bar to a 5-minute median session plus a second-evening return, and added a check with Turkish players before posting.
Replaced the unsourced Potion Craft line with the confirmed figure; softened Fluffy Onsen to the 61.7k–188k tracker range.
Re-stated the proven loop honestly: the counter loop is proven, the tease verb is not.
Downgraded proven loop and timing to ok and come-back-and-money to weak; lowered provenDemand, demand, instantPlay, monetization, marketability, momentum, culture and scopeFit.

winners.name: Teacup Tabby
winners.theme: Soft-body 'cats are liquid' container puzzle with a daily room
winners.hook: Cats are liquid: pick up a chonky cat and pour it into a teacup.
winners.oneLiner: A no-fail physics puzzle where you grab squishy cats by the scruff and drop, nudge and pile them into teacups, boots, sinks and too-small boxes until every cat in the room is sitting. Everyone gets the same Daily Room, with a spoiler-free result card to share.

clipStoryboard.shot: A huge orange cat dangles from a fingertip, stretched like mochi, above a tiny porcelain teacup on a sunny kitchen table. One questioning 'mrrp?'.
Release: the cat flops onto the rim, squashes wide and spills over both sides (a porcelain 'tink', then a soft 'blorp'). It looks impossible.
One gentle finger nudge. The cat starts to purr, its body softens and slowly glorps down into the cup until only a dome of fur is left above the rim.
Two ear tips pop up out of the cup ('pip, pip'), the eyes close in a slow blink, and a single warm chord rings. The camera eases in a little and holds.
A pull-back shows the whole room: three more cats already loafed in a boot, a sink and a fruit bowl. The purrs stack into one chord and the sunbeam warms.

provenLoop.loop: Short, no-fail physics puzzles where you fill containers and get a satisfying settle, plus a daily shared puzzle with a result card. Honest caveat: the research's cozy-puzzle niche has the lowest success rate (5.9% reach 1,000 reviews).

paidHits.name: Suika Game
paidHits.result: 10M+ downloads across Switch, iOS and Android (Aladdin X, July 2024); top Japanese Switch download of 2023 after streamers found it; iOS grossed almost $2M in its first three months (Siliconera; confirmed by search)

paidHits.name: A Little to the Left
paidHits.result: 999,999 copies by Nov 2023, at about $15; added a 'Daily Tidy' mode for return play (evergreen_other.json)

paidHits.name: Monkey Mart (Poki)
paidHits.result: About 300M plays on Poki, rated 4.6 from 3.79M votes; Poki serves 100M monthly players and 1B gameplays a month (management_tycoon.json). Shows the web portal pays off for a cute, instant format.

paidHits.name: Unpacking
paidHits.result: 100K in 10 days, 1M+ in year one: 'put things where they fit' satisfaction sells at a premium price (evergreen_other.json)

openTheme.demand: 'Cats are liquid' and 'if it fits, I sits' are some of the oldest and most durable cat memes. Cat content is the biggest pet category on TikTok and Shorts. The pool's If It Fits pitch scored 10 for clip appeal, the highest in the calibration table. Suika proved that a cute physics settle spreads by itself through streamers.
openTheme.supply: Fit My Cat (RedDeerGames, Switch/Xbox/Steam 2024) is a rigid grid packing puzzle with 90+ levels; reviews praise the calm but criticise controls that 'have a mind of their own'. It has no soft body and no pour. The exact gag already exists as a game-jam piece: 'Cats are liquid' (BitSummit Game Jam 2023) has you carry a plump cat on a spoon into a cup, so the joke is not ownable, only the execution is. Squishy Cats (iOS) is a hypercasual jelly-cat platformer; Box Cats Puzzle and 'If It Fits, It Sits' jam games are tiny prototypes. None makes the pour-and-sit a full game with a daily room.
openTheme.searched: Searched 'cats are liquid puzzle fit cat into container Steam', 'squishy cat physics puzzle soft body', '"If It Fits" cat game' and '"Fit My Cat" reviews'. Found Fit My Cat (grid, weak reviews), Squishy Cats (iOS hypercasual platformer), Box Cats Puzzle and several itch jam games. 'If It Fits' is taken by a cat board game and jam games, so the name is now Teacup Tabby, which turned up no existing game. Re-checked 'cats are liquid physics puzzle game fit cat in container' and found the BitSummit 2023 jam game with the same cup gag, plus Fit My Cat reviews (calm, but control complaints).

coreAction.verb: Scruff-grab and pour (pick up a cat, let it stretch, drop it, and let it ooze in)
coreAction.input: Touch: press on a cat, drag, lift the finger. Mouse: left-button drag. A second finger or right-click gives a short 'nudge' poke. One-handed and portrait-friendly.
coreAction.response: Within one frame of the press, the 3-4 body nodes nearest the finger attach to it with a soft spring, not a rigid pin. The cat's eyes snap wide, its ears flatten a little and its legs drop to dangle. Within about 80 ms the body stretches toward the finger like pulled mochi, while the rump lags behind under its own weight.
feedback: Animation, grab: eyes widen, pupils turn round, ears go back 15 degrees, and the four paws hang as pendulums that swing with drag velocity (follow-through). The face, ears, paws and tail are rigid sprites riding on the soft body, so the cat always reads as a cat rather than a blob.

Animation, carry: real soft-body stretch along the drag direction, clamped by a shader so it never goes past 1.8x length. The tail swishes against the motion. Fast shakes make the cheeks wobble, a joke players will discover.
Animation, land: on contact the body squashes to about 1.3x width (from the actual simulated nodes), then rebounds. A small 'paws out' frame plays on hard landings.

Animation, ooze: once more than about 55% of the cat is inside a container and it is nearly still, its 'relax' value ramps up over about 0.8 s. Internal pressure drops, the body flows to fill the shape, and the purr fades in. This is the deliberate slow beat after the fast drop.

Sound, layered: a 'mrrp?' on grab (pitch set by cat size, randomised by plus or minus 2 semitones, never the same twice in a row). A material hit on land: porcelain 'tink', cardboard 'thup', rubber-boot 'bwomp', enamel-sink 'dong'. A wet 'glorp' that rises in pitch as the cat sinks. Then a purr loop recorded from real cats.

Sound, chord: each cat that sits adds one note of a warm major-7th chord to the room's purr (C, E, G, B in cat order). When all cats sit, the chord resolves on a soft celesta. Players come to hear progress.
Particles: a few fur tufts at the rim on contact. Dust motes in the sunbeam swirl when a cat passes through. A single small heart or 'z' puff on the sit. Restrained, never confetti.

Camera: no shake, ever (cats are soft). On each sit the time scale drops to 0.35x for 120 ms, the camera pushes in 4% toward that cat and holds for 400 ms, then eases back. On the final sit the whole room's light warms over 1 s.
Haptics (mobile web): a 10 ms tick on grab, nothing while dragging, and a double tick [12, 40, 12] on the sit, timed with the ear pop.
UI: a faint dotted 'fill ring' inside each container shows how much of the cat is in, so 'why didn't it count?' never happens. Nudge count in a corner as a paw-print tally. No timer.
coreAction.payoff: The Sit: the cat sinks, two ear tips pop up out of the container, the eyes close in a slow blink and its purr joins the room's chord. When the last cat sits, the room exhales: light warms, the chord resolves, and a polaroid of the room drops into your album.
tuning: grabStiffness (finger spring k): low gives mochi stretch, high feels like carrying a brick. Start soft, then stiffen 20% for heavy cats so they don't drag across the floor

bodyPressure and relaxedPressure: how solid a cat is in the air versus how liquid it gets once it sits. This is the main personality knob (chonk 0.6 to 0.25, kitten 0.9 to 0.5, sphynx slippery with low friction)
relaxRampTime (0.5-1.2 s): length of the ooze beat. Too short and the payoff is lost, too long and it feels sluggish
sitThreshold (% inside, max speed): how forgiving 'fits' is
slowMoScale and slowMoDuration on a sit (0.35x / 120 ms)
maxStretchRatio before a cat 'pops' back to shape (1.8x)
containerFriction per material (porcelain slick, cardboard grippy)
earPopDelay after the sit (about 90 ms, so the ears land on the haptic tick)
sunbeamRelaxBonus: cats in a sunbeam relax faster, a mid-game puzzle tool
solverSubsteps and node count (24-32 perimeter nodes) for stability versus phone CPU
feelsBadIf: The cat is a featureless jelly blob. Keep the face, ears, paws and tail rigid and readable at all times, because the joke is that it's still clearly a cat.
Packed cats jitter or vibrate (soft-body solver instability). Use substeps, sleep resting nodes, and add damping once relaxed.
You pick up the wrong cat (Fit My Cat's main complaint). Pick the topmost face under the finger, highlight the grabbed cat's outline, and widen the hit area to the whole cat silhouette.
The finger covers the cat on a phone. Offset the grab point slightly above the touch and show the stretch.
Cats tunnel through thin container walls at speed. Use continuous collision and cap fall speed.
A sit doesn't register and players don't know why. The fill ring and a 'nearly' ear-twitch at 45% fix this.
It becomes a punishing optimisation puzzle. Keep it no-fail with no timer, and keep the nudge par only on the Daily Room card.
The cats look hurt or distressed when stretched. They should look surprised or unbothered, never in pain, so faces stay calm and stretch is limited.

clickMoment.first: Room 2. Room 1 was a cat and a big cardboard box. Room 2 shows a tiny teacup and a chonk three times its size, and the player assumes it can't work. They drop the cat anyway, it splats over the rim, they nudge once, and it slowly pours in until the ears pop up. 'Wait, it FITS?' That surprise, in under 60 seconds, is the hook and the clip.
clickMoment.deeper: Around the first chapter's end, players realise cats are a material. A relaxed chonk is a soft base you can pile a springy kitten onto, a sunbeam makes any cat runnier, and a sphynx slides into gaps nobody else fits. Puzzles turn into designing a cat pile. Attachment comes from the album: every solved room leaves a polaroid of your cats loafed in mismatched containers, and you name the regulars.

look.short: Warm gouache rooms · round ink-outlined cats pouring into teacups
look.vibe: Every room is a sunlit domestic corner painted in flat gouache: a kitchen table, a bathroom sink, a hallway of boots, all seen straight-on like a theatre set. The cats are simple round shapes with a confident brush-ink outline, flat fur colours, painted-on stripes that stretch with the body, and tiny triangular ears. A diagonal sunbeam crosses every room and the dust in it glitters. It should feel like a picture-book spread that wobbles.
look.signature: Two pointed ear tips and a closed-eye smile poking out of the top of a too-small teacup, in a sunbeam. That silhouette is the logo, the thumbnail and the Steam capsule.
references: Simon's Cat (line confidence)
Neko Atsume (cats in containers as a collection)
A Little to the Left (flat domestic tableau)
Suika Game (readable physics on a flat background)
Chi's Sweet Home picture-book colour
avoid: cluttered rooms where containers don't read at a glance

winners.sound: Real cat purrs and chirps (recorded or licensed from cat owners, credited in the game) are the instrument. Every sit adds a note to a warm major-7th purr chord over a quiet piano-and-celesta loop. Materials have their own voices (porcelain tink, cardboard thup, rubber bwomp), so a room of cats sounds different from the next.

timing.session: Short loops: one room takes 1-3 minutes with 2-5 cats. Chapters are themed homes of 8 rooms (Grandma's kitchen, a cat café, a laundrette), each ending with a 'cat parade' polaroid. The Daily Room takes 2-5 minutes, with a spoiler-free result card (cats, nudges, the container icons) to paste in a group chat.
timing.firstMinute: 0-15 s: one cat, one big box, and a hand-drawn arrow is the only tutorial. 15-45 s: the teacup and the chonk, splat, nudge, pour, ear pop. 45-60 s: a room with two cats and two containers where the obvious pairing is wrong. Swapping them is the first small 'aha'.
timing.marketWindow: Why now: cozy puzzle and physics-settle clips are at their peak after Suika's 10M+. Poki and CrazyGames reward instant, touch-first cute games. Dressmaker showed that a free itch prototype with 100k downloads can lead to a Steam hit. Best moments: put the free browser slice live for National Cat Day (Oct 29) or Japan's Cat Day (Feb 22, which sits next to the February Steam Next Fest, so the Steam demo goes into that Next Fest). Time the Steam 1.0 for International Cat Day (Aug 8), when cat-content creators look for something to post.

comeBack.short: A new Daily Room every morning, the same for everyone, with a nudge par and a result card your group chat compares.
comeBack.long: New cat temperaments (long cat, floof, sphynx, kitten litters) and new container materials keep changing the puzzles. The album of named cats in silly containers becomes a collection. A room editor lets players send each other 'impossible' rooms by link.

money.model: Free browser version (Daily Room plus the first chapter) on Poki/CrazyGames and your own site, with ads on the portal versions. Premium Steam/itch version with every chapter, the room editor and an album export.
money.price: Steam $7.99 (launch discount to $6.39); later a $2.99 chapter pack and a Switch port
money.evidence: Suika's iOS version grossed almost $2M in three months off a tiny puzzle (confirmed). A Little to the Left sold about 1M at about $15. Webfishing proved a $5 price spreads by word of mouth. Poki pays 100% of ad revenue on traffic you bring and 50/50 on theirs, and Monkey Mart reached about 300M Poki plays (management_tycoon.json). Calibration: 45% of cozy games at $20+ reach 1k reviews versus 2.7% under $5, so don't go below about $7; cozy puzzles specifically hit only 5.9%.

winners.proveItFirst: Build one browser room with one cat (a commissioned painted chonk: face, ears, paws and tail as separate sprites) and three containers: box, teacup, boot. Screen-record three vertical clips of the teacup pour and post them on TikTok and Shorts with the link in bio, plus an itch page. A yes is any clip over 100k views with 'what game is this / where can I play' comments, AND at least 40% of link visitors finishing all three containers, AND some players recording their own pour. If clips get views but people leave before the teacup, the feel needs work, not the idea.
winners.weakestLink: Off-track and copyable. The founder asked for proven loops rather than novelty toys, and this is the closest thing in the set to a toy: the whole pitch fits in a 5-second clip, the gag already exists as a jam game, and hypercasual studios can clone the pour fast if it goes viral. Cozy puzzles have the lowest hit rate (5.9%), a $7.99 puzzler only earns big if the Daily Room becomes a habit, and soft-body stability on cheap phone browsers is the technical risk.

provenLoop.note: Physics-settle (Suika 10M+) and fit-things-in puzzles (A Little to the Left ~1M, Unpacking 1M+) are proven, but a soft-body pour puzzle has no hit and cozy puzzles have the lowest hit rate (5.9%).

openTheme.note: Only weak competitors (Fit My Cat grid puzzle, a jam game, iOS hypercasual), but the cup gag itself already exists, so only the execution is ownable.

hook.note: 'Pour a cat into a teacup' needs no explanation, and the 5-second clip has no text.

moment.note: Ear tips popping out of a too-small cup is a perfect loop and thumbnail, and every player makes their own version.

feel.note: Grab, mochi stretch, splat, ooze and sit are specified with rigid readable features, a purr chord and haptic ticks; solver stability on cheap phones is the build risk.

click.note: The 'it fits?!' surprise lands in room 2, well inside a minute; cats as building material is the deeper click.

look.note: Gouache plus ink-outline cats is cheap to commission and the ears-in-a-teacup silhouette is an ownable mark.

timing.note: Cat days (Oct 29, Feb 22, Aug 8) and Next Fest give clear moments; cozy puzzles are evergreen, not rising.

comeBackAndMoney.note: Daily Room plus album gives a reason to return; the money is proven but modest (portal ads plus a small premium price).

critic.summary: The best pure clip in the set and the most link-friendly, with a feel spec that makes the meme physical. It can win as a web-first cozy puzzle with a daily habit, but it is off the founder's proven-genre brief, the gag already exists as a jam game, and a viral clip invites instant hypercasual clones.
fixesApplied: Added the BitSummit 2023 'Cats are liquid' jam game (same cup gag) to supply and lowered originality accordingly.
Confirmed Suika's 10M+ downloads and ~$2M iOS gross; replaced the unconfirmed '3.5/5' Fit My Cat score with what reviews actually say.
Added the research's 5.9% cozy-puzzle hit rate to the loop and money evidence, and named the off-track risk in the weakest link.
Lowered originality, provenDemand, marketability and momentum to sit next to the calibrated If It Fits row.

winners.name: Skein Street
winners.hook: Choose the yarn for someone's project, then they walk back in wearing it.
winners.oneLiner: Run a tiny wool shop on a windy island. Knitters bring a pattern and a reason (shown as a sketch: a hat and a fishing boat). You pick fibre and weight, speckle-dye a bare skein or build a colourway from a wall of cubbies, and crank each skein into a neat yarn cake on the ball winder. Days later they come back wearing the finished piece, and its photo goes on your show-and-tell wall.

clipStoryboard.shot: Side view of a small stone wool shop, rain streaking the window. A woman lays a pattern card on the counter: a sketched hat next to a tiny drawing of a fishing boat (no words). Door bell, rain hiss.

In the dye corner a bare cream skein lies in a tray; a hand squeezes sea-grey and gorse-yellow dye bottles over it in quick dots. The colours bloom and bleed into the wet wool. Heard: drip, a soft fizz.
Close on the ball winder: a circular drag cranks it, the ratchet clicks faster, the swift spins, and the speckles you just dropped wrap into a criss-cross yarn cake.
The cake pops off the winder with a hollow 'thup' and stands up flat-topped, speckled grey and gold. The customer squishes it and grins.
Door bell again. She's back with an old fisherman in a grey-and-gold speckled hat. An instant photo slides onto a wall already covered in finished jumpers, socks and blankets.

provenLoop.loop: Read a customer's request, choose the right thing from your stock, hand it over, restock and decorate (the Tiny Bookshop / Coffee Talk read-the-customer shop loop), with one tactile prep action and the customer's return as payoff.

paidHits.name: Tiny Bookshop
paidHits.result: 500,000+ copies after an Aug 2025 launch (200k+ in 12 days), 96% positive, physical and PS5 releases

paidHits.name: Coffee Talk
paidHits.result: ~369k units / $3.3M all platforms (VGI)

paidHits.name: Dressmaker (craft-audience proof, first-person)
paidHits.result: 400k+ wishlists, #9 Steam global top seller, budget recouped in under 24h (Sept 2026); itch prototype 100k+ downloads

paidHits.name: Bookshop Simulator (plain execution of a hobby shop)
paidHits.result: ~50.9k Steam copies / $488k, 93% (Raijin)

openTheme.demand: Tiny Bookshop showed that a hobby fandom will buy and market a recommendation shop (BookTok). Dressmaker's 2026 breakout shows the needle-craft audience is primed and buying right now, and the first-person-sims research notes crochet, knitting and sewing trending on TikTok with Gen Z. Knitters are famous for sharing finished objects, which is exactly this game's payoff.
openTheme.supply: No yarn or knitting shop game turned up in two rounds of searching. Knitwits (itch, Nov 2024) and Knit-Pick (GMTK jam 2025) are knitting-action toys, Yarn Sorting: Knitting Master is a mobile sort puzzle, and The Sims 4 has a knitting pack. Nearby hobby shops are arriving: Thrifty Business (May 2026, ~6.9k copies, low confidence), Piece by Piece (repair shop) and Tiny Bookshop followers; a plant-shop title (Leafy Corner) was reported by the designer search but not re-confirmed. The research itself expects Dressmaker clones to target knitting next, so 'unclaimed' may not last.

coreAction.verb: Wind (crank a chosen skein into a yarn cake on the ball winder)
coreAction.input: Phone: draw circles with one finger anywhere around the winder. Only the angle around the winder's centre counts, so circle size and jitter don't matter. Mouse: circular drag. Controller: rotate the right stick. Accessibility: hold to auto-wind at a fixed comfortable speed.
coreAction.response: The winder handle turns at your finger's angular speed from the first frame. The swift (the umbrella frame holding the hank) counter-rotates, the strand between them visibly travels and thrums, and the cake starts growing in its signature diagonal criss-cross wraps.
feedback: Pattern reveal: the cake texture is generated from the yarn's actual colourway, including the dye dots you dropped by hand in the speckle tray (an early unlock), so solid yarn wraps clean, speckled yarn scatters your own dots and variegated yarn pools into stripes. Every wind is a small reveal of how your colours behave.

Rhythm, not a meter: in the sweet speed band the cake grows crisp with a flat top. Crank too fast and the wraps go loose and lumpy ('yarn barf', a real knitter joke) and the strand slaps. Too slow and it simply takes longer. You see the quality on the cake itself.

Sound: the plastic ratchet goes 'tk-tk-tk' at a rate tied to speed (granular, so it never machine-guns), a soft wool hiss on the strand, the swift's wooden creak and a hollow 'thup' when the cake pops off.

Animation: the swift's arms flex slightly under tension, the strand wobbles with a sine amplitude tied to speed, the last tail whips round the cake (follow-through), and the finished cake squashes 10% as it stands on the counter, then settles.
Haptics: a light tick per full revolution and a firmer pulse on pop-off.
Camera: a 300 ms gentle push-in on the finished cake, then pull back to show it standing in the customer's colourway line-up.
Particles: fine fibre motes drift through the window light, more at higher speed. Mohair throws a halo.
Customer: they lean in during winding, and on pop-off they squish the cake (a 4-frame squash) and react to the colours, not to a score.
Fibre differences: each fibre sounds and moves differently. Chunky wool is slow and plush, sock yarn fast and tight, mohair fuzzy and quiet, so the same gesture feels different across stock.
coreAction.payoff: Two to four cakes standing side by side on the counter next to the pattern card, the customer's face lighting up at the combination, and, later, the door bell and the finished piece walking in.
tuning: Sweet-spot angular speed band and its width: how much rhythm skill matters
Revolutions per skein (keep each wind about 3–4 seconds): chore versus pleasure
Barf threshold and how lumpy a loose cake looks: how much a sloppy wind shows
Ratchet click rate versus speed: how fast feels fast
Pop-off squash amount and push-in duration: how much each cake weighs
Number of skeins per order (1–4): length of each customer
In-game days until a customer returns with the finished object: anticipation
Hard-rule strictness (weight and fibre fit) versus soft taste (colour): how quiz-like matching feels
Speckle dye bloom radius and bleed time: how much a dropped dot spreads into the wet wool before it sets.
feelsBadIf: Winding becomes a chore. Keep it short, let a hired helper auto-wind bulk orders later, and keep hand-winding for the colourways you care about.
Circle detection is janky on a phone. Read only the angle around the centre, smoothed over 3 frames, and accept any radius.
Matching is a quiz with one right answer. Weight and fibre have real rules, but colour has many good answers and the customer reacts to taste.
Craft details are wrong. Knitters will notice, so fibre, weight and yardage logic is checked by real knitters.
The return payoff takes too long. The first customer must come back inside the first session.
Finished objects look generic. Each return photo has to show the exact colours you chose, in the item's pattern.

clickMoment.first: Within the first minute: the first customer wants 'a warm hat for my dad who fishes'. You pull a chunky sea-grey wool and a stripe of yellow, crank the winder, watch the speckles wrap into the cake, and it pops off into her hands. Then, at the end of that first short day, she comes back with Da wearing it, in your colours. That's when it clicks: what you choose becomes real.
clickMoment.deeper: A few days in, your show-and-tell wall is a quilt of things that exist because of you. Regulars come back with bigger and riskier projects (Morag's first-ever jumper, a blanket for a new baby), and a customer asks for 'whatever you'd choose', trusting your taste. Mastery is building colourways that surprise people and work.

look.short: Side-view island wool shop · painted 2D · rainbow cubby wall against grey sea mist
look.vibe: A narrow side-on wool shop on a Shetland-like island: whitewashed stone, a deep-set window with rain and sea mist outside, and one whole wall of wooden cubbies stuffed with yarn sorted into a rainbow gradient. The world outside is soft greys and greens, and every bit of saturated colour lives in the yarn, so the wall glows like a paint swatch. Customers are chunky, bundled-up islanders in their own hand-knits, drawn in painted 2D with soft texture. The show-and-tell wall of instant photos slowly fills the other side of the shop.
look.signature: A floor-to-ceiling rainbow wall of yarn cubbies glowing inside a grey, rain-misted stone shop
references: Tiny Bookshop (warm painted shop, customer vignettes)
Fair Isle knitting colourwork (the palette logic)
Real local yarn shops' cubby walls (the thumbnail)
Coffee Talk (single-room side view with characters at a counter)
avoid: Generic 'cottagecore' pastels everywhere: keep colour in the yarn only
Fake knitting terms or impossible yarn

winners.sound: Weather and wool. Rain on glass, wind under the door and the sea far off are the bed. The ball-winder ratchet is the signature sound, and every fibre has its own hiss. A slow fiddle-and-harp folk score commissioned from a musician lifts when a customer returns wearing your colours, with the shop bell as its downbeat.

timing.session: A customer takes 30–90 seconds (read, pick, wind, hand over). A shop day is 4–6 customers plus one or two returns with finished objects, ending as you flip the sign and see the day's photo on the wall. Between days you restock from island dyers whose seasonal colourways change. On Steam, the arc runs through the island's year (lambing, summer tourists, a wool-week festival, winter knit-alongs), with regulars' small stories carrying across it.
timing.firstMinute: The door bell rings as the game opens, the first customer is already talking, and the pattern card asks a simple fibre-and-colour question. Pick, wind, pop, squish, all inside 60 seconds. Her return with the finished hat lands before the first day ends.
timing.marketWindow: Knitting is an autumn and winter hobby, and the Dressmaker breakout (Sept 2026) has just shown the craft audience will buy. Ship the browser slice and clips into knitting TikTok and r/knitting as knitting season starts, take the Steam demo to the October or February Next Fest, and launch into the next autumn, ideally around Shetland Wool Week, with knitting YouTubers ('knittubers') as the streamer channel.

comeBack.short: Someone you served yesterday is coming back today with what they made, and the dyers have a new seasonal colourway in.
comeBack.long: The show-and-tell wall becomes a collection of your taste, regulars' projects grow from scarves to heirloom jumpers, the shop expands (a dye pot out back, a knit-night table, a second room), and the island's year changes what people ask for.

money.model: Free browser slice as the hook test, a paid itch or Ko-fi supporter build, then a premium Steam version with a demo, plus later colourway or pattern-book DLC and a console port if it sells
money.evidence: Tiny Bookshop (~$20) sold 500k+, Coffee Talk (~$13) ~369k / $3.3M, and Dressmaker ($14.99) recouped its budget in under 24h. 45.2% of $20+ cozy games reach 1,000 reviews versus 2.7% under $5 (budget confound noted). Even a plain hobby-shop execution (Bookshop Simulator) made ~$488k.

winners.proveItFirst: Build a one-customer browser toy: pattern card, a small cubby wall, the winder with the barf-versus-neat cake, and the finished-hat return photo. Post a vertical clip of the winding and the return on knitting TikTok and r/knitting, with the playable link. A yes is knitters sharing it themselves (stitches, duets, people posting what colourway they'd have picked), a front-page r/knitting thread, and at least 10% of slice players signing up for the Steam wishlist or Discord. If they only critique craft accuracy, fix that first.
winners.weakestLink: Clip power and content volume. The research is blunt that cozy shops without a clip-able hook sell under 10k (Thrifty Business ~6.9k), and this game's best moment (the customer returning in your colours) is emotional rather than instantly satisfying; the speckle-dye-and-wind beat has to carry the clips. Every customer also needs writing and every return a finished-object illustration in the chosen colours, knitters will punish wrong craft details, and Dressmaker clones are expected to arrive in knitting.

provenLoop.note: Tiny Bookshop (500k+) and Coffee Talk (~369k) prove the read-the-customer shop, but there are fewer hits than for restoration or counter loops.

openTheme.note: No yarn shop game found in two searches, while the needle-craft audience is surging after Dressmaker; clones are a future, not current, threat.

hook.note: 'They come back wearing it' is warm and clear, but the payoff needs two scenes separated in time, so the 5-second clip is weaker than the others'.

moment.note: The speckle-dye-and-wind reveal and the cake pop-off are pleasant and real ASMR formats, but not as instantly shareable as a split shoe or a sliced loaf.

feel.note: The angle-only crank with a sweet-speed band and fibre-specific sound is solid, but the most frequent decision (choosing yarn) is a selection, not a physical action.

click.note: The first wind lands inside a minute; the bigger click (the return in your colours) arrives at the end of the first day, not the first minute.

look.note: The rainbow cubby wall glowing inside a grey, rain-misted stone shop is an instantly recognisable thumbnail.

timing.note: Knitting season and the post-Dressmaker moment fit, but the same moment invites knitting clones.

comeBackAndMoney.note: Returning customers are a real reason to come back and $14.99 premium has precedent, but there is no portal income and the ceiling depends on clips that are harder to make.

critic.summary: An empty hobby-shop theme with a proven Tiny Bookshop-style loop and a lovely thumbnail, aimed at a craft audience that is buying right now. It can win if knitters adopt it as their own the way BookTok adopted Tiny Bookshop; it dies the way Thrifty Business did, as a well-made cozy shop without a clip that spreads.

winners.name: Tangle Hill
winners.theme: Cozy co-op hangout (not fishing): kite flying
winners.hook: Paint a kite, send a link, and fly with your friends on one windy hill. Try not to tangle.
winners.oneLiner: A cheap 1-8 player hangout on a windy hill. You draw your own kite, catch the gusts you can see rolling through the grass, and fly next to friends whose lines hum like strings. Sooner or later two kites cross, spiral together and land in the kite-eating tree.

clipStoryboard.shot: Low angle from the grass: four hand-drawn kites against a huge blue sky (a frog, a badly drawn cat, a heart, a crayon dinosaur), each trailing a ribbon tail. Wind and a soft chord of humming lines.
A wave of brighter grass rolls up the hill toward the players. The frog kite catches it, surges up, and its line's hum jumps an octave.
The cat kite drifts into the frog kite's line. The lines cross, twist, and both kites start spiralling around each other faster and faster. Two players' voices: 'no no no NO'.
Both kites corkscrew into a huge oak that is already full of dozens of other players' kites. Leaves burst out. A crow lands on the cat kite.
Cut to the tiny figures on the hill doing a group 'facepalm' emote, then the sun sets and the remaining kites light up as lanterns.

coreAction.verb: Pull the line (feel the wind through the string and catch the gusts)
coreAction.input: Mouse: hold left button to pull the line in, release to let it run out, and move the mouse left/right to steer the kite's nose. Touch: hold anywhere to pull and slide left/right to steer. Controller: right trigger to pull (analogue, so half-pressure gives half-pull), left stick to steer, and rumble carries line tension.
coreAction.response: On press, the line snaps from a lazy sagging curve to straight in the same frame. The kite's nose dips for about 60 ms (anticipation), then it climbs. The line's hum starts immediately at a pitch set by tension. Your character leans back with both fists at their chest. Release, and the line visibly bellies out and the hum falls away to a flutter.
feedback: Line physics: a 40-segment verlet rope with sag that responds to tension. Pulled, it goes straight and bright; slack, it droops into a soft catenary. The line is the main readout, so players read tension from it rather than from a meter.

Kite animation: the sail fabric bows under load (vertex squash along the spine), and the ribbon tail (a separate rope with cloth ribbons) whips and lags with follow-through. On a gust catch the kite lunges upward, stretching 10% along its climb, then settles.
Character: leans back against tension (rig blend by tension 0-1), stumbles a step forward when a strong gust yanks, plants their feet when you hold. Small but sells the force.

Visible wind: gusts are telegraphed 0.8-1.2 s ahead as a bright wave rolling up the grass, petals and dandelion seeds streaming, and cloud shadows racing. You see the wind coming, which turns waiting into anticipation.

Sound, the signature: each line is a bowed-string or Aeolian-harp tone with pitch tied to tension. Each player's line is tuned to a different note of a pentatonic scale, so four friends flying make a shifting chord. Layers on top: fabric flutter (rate tied to airspeed), a soft rope creak at max tension, and a wind bed.
Gust catch payoff sound: pulling inside the gust window plays a rising 'whumph' as the sail fills, the hum jumps an octave for 1.5 s, and a high harmonic shimmers.

Camera: third person behind the flyer, lifting and tilting up 6-8 degrees when your kite climbs, so the sky gets bigger. A slight FOV widen (2-3 degrees) on a gust catch. No shake except a tiny one on a tree crash.
Haptics: controller rumble at low frequency scales with tension, plus a sharp pulse on a gust catch and on a line touch. Mobile web vibrates only on a catch and on a tangle start.

Particles: dandelion seeds and blossom streaming in gusts, a puff of leaves on a tree crash, and a short ribbon of sparkles trailing the tail during tricks (loops leave a fading ribbon, so players can draw hearts in the sky).
UI: almost none. A small altitude ribbon on the line near your hands, and the gust count shown as knots on your line.
coreAction.payoff: Catching a big gust perfectly: your kite surges high above everyone else's, the camera lifts to a huge sky, and your line's note rings out an octave higher over your friends' chord. The social payoff is the tangle spiral into the kite-eating tree, which everyone laughs at.
tuning: tensionToLift curve: how much pulling climbs versus stalls. The main skill knob, kept generous for beginners
steadyWindFloor: a minimum lift so a kite never falls out of the sky just because you did nothing (no death spiral)
gustTelegraphLead (0.8-1.2 s) and gustWindow (how early or late a pull still counts)
gustFrequency and strength per hill and time of day
lineLengthMax and reelSpeed
tangleTwistThreshold: how many crossings before lines lock into a spiral (1.5 twists), and autoUntangleTime (about 6 s) so tangles never trap anyone
humPitchRange per player and the scale (pentatonic, so any combination sounds pleasant)
tailDrag: longer tails are more stable but slower, which makes tails both a cosmetic and a handling choice
cameraLift degrees per 10 m of altitude
netInterpolationBuffer (about 100 ms) for other players' kites
feelsBadIf: Beginners can't keep the kite up and it keeps crashing. Use a steady-wind floor and an auto-stabilising assist that fades as you play.
Wind is invisible and gusts feel random. Always telegraph them in the grass, petals and clouds.
Other players' kites stutter or teleport. Interpolate, and simulate remote lines locally from synced kite positions.
Tangles are used to grief people. Auto-untangle after about 6 s, keep private link lobbies as the default, and add a 'wide sky' option that turns off line collisions with non-friends.
Drawn kites are used for offensive images in public lobbies. Public lobbies show non-friends' kites as plain colours unless you opt in, with report and block.
The line looks like a stiff stick. Never draw it as straight segments without sag or vibration.
There's nothing to do after ten minutes. Gust medals, tricks, ribbon drawings, lantern dusk and seasonal hills give structure without goals.

clickMoment.first: In the first 20 seconds your kite sags and wobbles. Then a bright wave of grass comes rolling up the hill. You pull just as it reaches you, the kite leaps into the sky and your line sings an octave higher. 'I caught the wind.' In the first minute a friend joins from the link and their line hums a second note under yours.
clickMoment.deeper: The first real tangle: you and a friend realise you can untwist by circling opposite ways, and you talk each other through it (and fail into the tree). Later, at dusk, four friends hold their lines at different tensions on purpose to play a chord. The hill becomes a shared instrument and the group's place, and the tree slowly fills with your group's crashed kites, which stay there between sessions.

look.short: A huge sky over one rounded green hill · crayon-drawn kites with long ribbon tails
look.vibe: Two-thirds of every frame is sky: deep cobalt at the top fading to warm haze, with big soft painted cumulus clouds. The hill is a smooth, low-poly rounded green dome with wind-brushed grass shaded in two tones and a single enormous oak on the shoulder, its branches full of other people's kites. Players are small, round, faceless-ish figures in knitted hats. The kites are the only hand-drawn, wobbly-line things in the world, so player art pops.
look.signature: The kite lines: one bright, sun-catching thread from each tiny figure to its kite, drawn thin and glowing against the sky. Plus the oak tree stuffed with crashed kites.

Alto's Adventure (sky gradients)
Sky: Children of the Light (a sky as a social space)
Peanuts' kite-eating tree
Studio Ghibli wind in grass (Kiki's Delivery Service hillside)

winners.sound: The game sounds like an Aeolian harp: every kite line is a living string whose pitch follows its tension, tuned so any group of players makes a pleasant pentatonic chord. Under it are wind, fabric flutter, skylarks and a distant town bell at dusk. Music is sparse acoustic guitar and harmonium that only fades in during lantern hour.

timing.session: Micro loop: 20-40 s cycles of waiting, a visible gust, a pull and a soar. Meso loop: a 3-5 minute 'wind spell' with a gust medal goal (catch 5 big gusts, do a loop, write a heart in ribbon) that earns tail ribbons and fabrics. Macro loop: an in-game day of about 20 minutes on the hill, ending in lantern dusk when kites glow and everyone releases a sky lantern together. Then the lobby keeps hanging out or leaves.
timing.firstMinute: 0-10 s: paint a kite on a diamond template with three crayon colours (or skip with a preset). 10-30 s: the kite lifts off your hands and the first telegraphed gust arrives and is caught. 30-60 s: a 'share this hill' link button. A friend's kite appears beside yours, the two hums meet, and their line drifts suspiciously close to yours.
timing.marketWindow: Why now: the 'more games like Webfishing' demand is still unmet by small games, cheap co-op friendslop is the breakout pattern of 2025-26, and Open World / co-op niches keep above-average odds. Best moments: test the browser link around Makar Sankranti/Uttarayan (Jan 14), when kite clips flood social feeds. Put the Steam demo into the February Steam Next Fest. Launch 1.0 in spring kite season (late March to April, around Washington's Blossom Kite Festival and Weifang), with a seasonal autumn hill update timed to Guatemala's giant kites on Nov 1.

comeBack.short: Your friends are there, or their ghost kites are: a daily 'wind of the day' (a named weather pattern with its own gusts and a medal) and lantern dusk give a reason to meet up, and the tree keeps your group's crashed kites.
comeBack.long: Seasonal hills (cherry-blossom spring, beach, autumn harvest, a snowy winter hill), new kite frames (box, delta, giant festival kites flown by two players at once), a growing wardrobe of tails and fabrics, and the group's own tree full of trophies. A real group ritual, like Webfishing's lobbies.

money.model: Free browser slice (2-4 players by link, one hill, limited kite frames) to spread. Premium Steam version with 8-player lobbies, all hills, kite frames and Steam Workshop kite designs. Optional cosmetic supporter pack.
money.price: Steam $5.99, a 4-pack friend bundle, and a $3.99 supporter pack (soundtrack plus festival kite frames)
money.evidence: Webfishing sold an estimated 1.3M (Raijin) to ~5M copies at $5 as a solo project, and Rusty's Retirement at about $7 sold 500K+ (evergreen_other.json). PEAK (about $8) sold 5M+ in about a month, confirmed, showing cheap co-op comedy breaks out through streamers. Below $5 a game without a background hook rarely reaches 1k reviews (2.7%), so stay at about $6, not $3.

winners.proveItFirst: Build a single-player browser toy first: one hill, one kite, visible gusts and the singing line, with no netcode. Add 'ghost kites': replays of the last few visitors' flights (and their drawn kites, friends-only by default) drifting in the same sky, which gives social presence with no live servers. Post vertical clips of a gust catch with the hum, and a two-kite tangle played by you in two browser windows. A yes is clip comments tagging friends ('we need this', '@x play with me') at over 5% of comments, plus solo players staying over 3 minutes on average with nothing to do but fly. Only then add link lobbies and test with 20 friend groups; the yes there is groups coming back unprompted the next day.
winners.weakestLink: It depends on friends and on emergent clips you can't plan. Solo, it is a lovely ten-minute toy (ghost kites help, but don't replace friends), and retention only exists if groups adopt the hill as their hangout, which can't be proven until real groups play. Live netcode for crossing ropes plus moderating drawn kites is the hardest engineering and ops in this set for one person, and the exact concept already exists as an itch prototype.

provenLoop.note: The cheap hangout around one relaxing verb is proven by Webfishing (1.3M+ est., solo, $5), and PEAK shows cheap co-op comedy spreads, but no kite game has sold.

openTheme.note: No cozy kite hangout on Steam, but the same concept exists on itch (Come Fly With Me), Outbound has 4-player co-op kites, and a 16-player kite game is coming.

hook.note: 'Draw a kite, send a link, don't tangle' is instantly understood, and the clip works without text.

moment.note: The tangle spiral into a tree full of kites is a systemic group-laugh clip, and hand-drawn kites make every clip unique.

feel.note: A singing line with pitch from tension, telegraphed gusts with a timing window, rope sag as the readout and analogue-trigger rumble make the pull physical.

click.note: Catching the first visible gust lands within 30 s, but the real click (a friend's line humming under yours) needs a second person.

look.note: Big sky plus glowing threads is clear and cheap with low-poly packs, but low-poly hills are a familiar look; player drawings carry the distinctiveness.

timing.note: Real kite calendar moments (Uttarayan, spring festivals) and Next Fest, but kite culture is regional and 'more Webfishing' demand is two years old.

comeBackAndMoney.note: Retention lives entirely on friend groups adopting the hill, which can't be shown before netcode exists, and a $5.99 price needs a streamer moment to matter.

critic.summary: A fresh relaxing verb for the under-served cheap co-op hangout space, with a singing line that is genuinely new game feel and a tangle that writes its own clips. It can win the way Webfishing did if groups adopt the hill; it dies as a pretty solo toy, or on rope netcode and drawn-kite moderation that one person can't support.
